Research by Onk T, Van Cosburgh J, and Van Dasselaar T et al. in 2020 demonstrated that tapentadol treatment provides long-term pain relief for patients with chronic low back pain and is associated with reduced segmental sensitization. 2. Vondrackova D, Leyendecker P, and Meissner W et al. in 2008 evaluated the analgesic efficacy and safety of oxycodone combined with naloxone in prolonged-release tablets for patients with moderate to severe chronic pain, showing significant benefits. 3. Vorsanger GJ, Xiang J, and Gana TJ et al. in 2008 studied extended-release tramadol (tramadol ER) for chronic low back pain, finding it effective in managing pain symptoms. 4. Webster LR, Butera PG, and Moran LV et al. in 2006 conducted a randomized controlled trial on Oxytrex, which minimized physical dependence while providing effective analgesia for low back pain. 5. Weil AJ, Masters ET, and Barsdorf AI et al. in 2017 reported that treatment with ALO-02 (extended-release oxycodone and sequestered naltrexone) improved patient-reported health-related quality of life, work productivity, and activity impairment in moderate-to-severe chronic low back pain. 6. The 2020 WHO guidelines recommend non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults within primary and community care settings. 7. Wen W, Sitar S, and Lynch SY et al. in 2015 assessed the efficacy and safety of single-entity, once-daily hydrocodone tablets in patients with uncontrolled moderate-to-severe chronic low back pain through a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. 8. Yarlas A, Miller K, and Wen W et al. in 2013 conducted a placebo-controlled study on the 7-day buprenorphine transdermal system, showing improvements in health-related quality of life for opioid-naïve patients with moderate-to-severe chronic low back pain. 9. Yarlas A, Miller K, and Wen W et al. in 2016 found no diminished response to buprenorphine transdermal system treatment in chronic low back pain patients with depression. 10. Yarlas A, Miller K, and Wen W et al. in 2015 demonstrated that the buprenorphine transdermal system reduced functional interference in chronic low back pain compared to placebo. 11. Khoromi S, Cui L, and Nackers L et al. in 2007 compared morphine, nortriptyline, and their combination versus placebo in patients with chronic lumbar root pain, showing significant pain relief. 12. Ionescu AM, Manolescu BN, and Popa R et al. in 2015 explored the effects of tramadol treatment on aerobic exercise capacity in individuals with chronic non-specific low back pain. 13. Birbara CA, Puopolo AD, and Munoz DR et al. in 2003 evaluated etoricoxib, a COX-2 selective inhibitor, for chronic low back pain, finding improvements in pain and disability in a randomized, placebo-controlled trial. 14. Katz N, Borenstein DG, and Birbara C et al. in 2011 assessed the efficacy and safety of tanezumab for chronic low back pain, demonstrating significant pain reduction. 15. Kivitz AJ, Gimbel JS, and Bramson C et al. in 2013 compared tanezumab to naproxen for chronic low back pain, showing superior efficacy of tanezumab. 16. Pallay RM, Seger W, and Adler JL et al. in 2004 reported that etoricoxib reduced pain and disability while improving quality of life in chronic low back pain patients over a 3-month randomized trial. 17. Berry H, Bloom B, and Hamilton EB et al. in 1982 compared naproxen sodium, diflunisal, and placebo for chronic back pain, finding significant pain relief with both medications. 18. Ghosh P, Taylor TKF, and Meachin AD in 1981 conducted a double-blind crossover trial of indomethacin, flurbiprofen, and placebo for lumbar spondylosis, showing efficacy of the medications. 19. Gurrell R, Dua P, and Feng G et al. in 2018 evaluated PF-06372865, a selective GABAA modulator, in chronic low back pain patients, demonstrating its potential in pain management. 20. Konno S, Oda N, and Ochiai T et al. in 2016 conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of duloxetine monotherapy in Japanese patients with chronic low back pain, showing significant pain reduction. 21. Sklarjevski V, Desai D, and Liu-Seifert H et al. in 2010 demonstrated the efficacy and safety of duloxetine in chronic low back pain patients in a randomized, double-blind trial. 22. Atkinson JH, Slater MA, and Caparelli EV et al. in 2007 evaluated noradrenergic and serotonergic antidepressants for chronic back pain, showing significant reductions in pain intensity. 23. Dickens C, Jayson M, and Sutton C et al. in 2000 explored the relationship between pain and depression in chronic low back pain patients treated with paroxetine, finding improvements in both symptoms. 24. Johnson K, Chatterjee N, and Noor N et al. in 2011 assessed duloxetine versus placebo in chronic low back pain patients, showing significant pain relief. 25. Schnitzer TJ et al. in 2012 evaluated milnacipran for chronic neuropathic low back pain, demonstrating its efficacy in a clinical trial. 26. Schukro RP, Oehmke MJ, and Geroldinger A et al. in 2016 conducted a crossover trial of duloxetine for chronic low back pain with a neuropathic component, showing significant pain reduction. 27. Atkinson HJ, Slater MA, and Williams RA et al. in 1998 evaluated nortriptyline for chronic low back pain in a placebo-controlled trial, finding significant pain relief. 28. Pheasant H, Bursk A, and Goldfarb J et al. in 1983 conducted a double-blind crossover study of amitriptyline for chronic low back pain, showing its efficacy in pain management. 29. Alcoff J, Jones E, and Rust P et al. in 1982 evaluated imipramine for chronic low back pain in a controlled trial, demonstrating significant pain relief. 30. Loldrup D, Langemark M, and Hansen HJ et al. in 1989 compared clomipramine and mianserin for chronic idiopathic pain syndrome, showing efficacy in a placebo-controlled study.
